title: Running the machine backwards
objectives: Find an inverse function by undoing steps in reverse order.
See the graph of an inverse as a reflection in $y = x$.

screens.prose: The machine $f$ doubles its input, then adds 3. A number went in and 17 came out.
screens.question: What went in?

hints.text: What was the number just before 3 was added?
The middle cell held the number before 3 was added.
Before adding 3 it was 14. Before doubling it was 7.

feedback.correct: Undo the last step first: $17 - 3 = 14$, then $14 \div 2 = 7$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Undo the adding first, then the doubling.

byKey.forward: You fed 17 into the machine. We need the number that came out as 17, so we run it backwards.
byKey.order: You halved first, then subtracted 3. Undo the last step first: subtract 3, then halve.
byKey.half: You undid the doubling but not the adding. Take off the 3 first.
byKey.sub: 14 is the number before 3 was added. It was doubled from something.

explain.text: Undo the last step first: $17 - 3 = 14$. Then undo the doubling: $14 \div 2 = 7$. Check: $2 \times 7 + 3 = 17$.

screens.prose: P sits on the graph of $f(x) = 2x + 3$. Q takes P's coordinates and swaps them. The dashed line is $y = x$. Drag P and watch Q.
screens.question: Drag P until P and Q land on the same spot.

hints.text: P and Q coincide when P's two coordinates are equal.
That happens on the dashed line $y = x$.

feedback.correct: At $(-3, -3)$ swapping changes nothing, so P and Q meet.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find where the graph of $f$ meets the dashed line.

explain.text: Swapping coordinates mirrors a point in the line $y = x$. A point on that line is its own mirror image, so P and Q meet at $(-3, -3)$. As P moves, Q traces a mirror copy of the graph.

screens.prose: Q's path is the graph of the machine run backwards, the **inverse** of $f$, written $f^{-1}$. Since $f(7) = 17$, we have $f^{-1}(17) = 7$.
screens.question: Use $f(x) = 2x + 3$. What is $f^{-1}(11)$?

hints.text: Which input makes $f$ give out 11?
Read the inverse graph, or undo $f$ step by step.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Undo the adding of 3, then the doubling.

byKey.forward: You worked out $f(11)$. The inverse asks which input $f$ turns into 11.
byKey.order: You halved before subtracting. Undo the last step first: $11 - 3$, then halve.
byKey.recip: You worked out $\tfrac{1}{f(11)}$. The $-1$ in $f^{-1}$ means run backwards, not divide.

screens.prose: The two graphs mirror each other in $y = x$. Here is a new function, $g(x) = \tfrac{1}{2}x + 1$, with the point $(4, 3)$ on it.
screens.question: Drag P to the matching point on the graph of $g^{-1}$.

hints.text: Swap the two coordinates.
Mirror the point in the dashed line.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Swap the $x$ and $y$ of $(4, 3)$.

byKey.flip-x: You reflected in the $x$-axis. The inverse reflects in the line $y = x$, which swaps the coordinates.
byKey.flip-y: You reflected in the $y$-axis. The inverse reflects in the line $y = x$.

explain.text: $g(4) = 3$, so $g^{-1}(3) = 4$, which is the point $(3, 4)$. Swapping coordinates reflects in $y = x$. Every point of $g$ does the same.

screens.prose: Take $f(x) = x + 4$. A classmate reads the $-1$ in $f^{-1}(6)$ as a power, and works out $\dfrac{1}{f(6)}$.
screens.question: What is $f^{-1}(6)$?

hints.text: Which input does $f$ turn into 6?
Find 6 in the $f(x)$ column.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for the input that $f$ turns into 6.

byKey.recip: You read the $-1$ as a power and worked out $\tfrac{1}{f(6)} = \tfrac{1}{10}$. $f^{-1}$ means run $f$ backwards.
byKey.recip-input: You took $\tfrac{1}{6}$. The inverse asks which input gives 6, not one over 6.
byKey.forward: You ran 6 forwards through $f$. Run it backwards: subtract 4.

explain.text: $f^{-1}(6)$ is the input that $f$ turns into 6, and $f(2) = 6$. So $f^{-1}(6) = 2$, not $\tfrac{1}{10}$. In $f^{-1}$ the $-1$ is a label meaning backwards.

screens.prose: Now $f(x) = x^2$, the squaring machine. It gave out 9.
screens.question: What went in?

options.why: You found one input. $(-3)^2 = 9$ as well, so 3 is not the only possibility.
You found one input. $3^2 = 9$ as well, so $-3$ is not the only possibility.
You squared 9. We need the input that gives 9.

hints.text: How many times does the dashed line meet the curve?
The line $y = 9$ crosses the curve twice.

feedback.correct: Two inputs give 9, so running backwards cannot choose.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the points where the dashed line meets the curve.

explain.text: Both 3 and $-3$ give out 9, so running backwards has two answers. A machine that sends two inputs to one output has no inverse. Allow only $x \ge 0$, and the inverse exists: it is $\surd{x}$.

screens.prose: To undo a machine, undo its steps in reverse order. $$y = 2x + 3 \;\Rightarrow\; x = \frac{y - 3}{2} \;\Rightarrow\; f^{-1}(x) = \frac{x - 3}{2}$$ Each point $(a, b)$ on $f$ becomes $(b, a)$ on $f^{-1}$: a reflection in $y = x$.
screens.question: $(2, 9)$ is on the graph of $f$. Which point is on the graph of $f^{-1}$?

options.why: You reflected in the $y$-axis. The inverse swaps the two coordinates.
You took one over the output. $f^{-1}$ runs backwards; it does not divide.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Swap the coordinates.

explain.text: $f(2) = 9$ means $f^{-1}(9) = 2$. So $(9, 2)$ is on $f^{-1}$: the same point with its coordinates swapped.

screens.prose: Find the inverse of $f(x) = 5x - 2$. Write $y = 5x - 2$, solve for $x$, then swap the letters.
screens.question: Write $f^{-1}(x)$.

hints.text: Undo the last step first: add 2 to both sides.
$y + 2 = 5x$, so $x = \tfrac{y + 2}{5}$. Now swap the letters.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add 2 first, then divide by 5.

byKey.same-order: You divided by 5 before adding 2. Undo in reverse: the subtraction came last, so undo it first.
byKey.recip: You wrote $\tfrac{1}{f(x)}$. The inverse runs the machine backwards.

explain.text: Adding 2 undoes the subtraction: $y + 2 = 5x$. Dividing by 5 undoes the multiplying: $x = \tfrac{y + 2}{5}$. So $f^{-1}(x) = \tfrac{x + 2}{5}$; check $f^{-1}(f(1)) = f^{-1}(3) = 1$.

screens.prose: You buy 250 shares at £8.40 and pay £12.50 commission. Your P&L at sale price $S$ is $P(S) = 250(S - 8.40) - 12.50$ pounds.
screens.question: At what sale price does your P&L reach £300.00?

hints.text: Run the P&L machine backwards from 300.
Find where the P&L line meets the dashed target.
Add back 12.50 to get 312.50. Divide by 250 to get 1.25. Add 8.40.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Undo the steps of $P$ in reverse order.

byKey.nofee: You left out the commission. You need £312.50 of gain to finish £300.00 ahead.
byKey.subfee: You took the commission off the target. It has to be earned back, so add it: £312.50.
byKey.forward: You fed 300 into $P$ as a price. Run the machine backwards from a P&L of 300.

explain.text: Undo in reverse: $300 + 12.50 = 312.50$, then $312.50 \div 250 = 1.25$, then $1.25 + 8.40 = 9.65$. So $P^{-1}(300) = 9.65$: sell at £9.65. The inverse turns a target P&L into the price you need.

ideas: The inverse $f^{-1}$ runs a machine backwards: undo the last step first.
The graph of $f^{-1}$ is the mirror image of $f$ in $y = x$: $(a, b)$ becomes $(b, a)$.
A machine that sends two inputs to one output has no inverse unless we restrict its inputs.

quiz.question: Which one has no inverse?
